doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Ears, left hand and the sound of the song
summary: Tactile association on the fingerboard versus hearing, and Hank Jones keeping the sound of the song through changing voicings.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Is some of that, when you’re talking about your ears are getting bigger and they’re telling you where to go, is it also some of that like almost attached to your left hand? Like okay I hear this coming and I know that boom, that’s a string down and down a position or something.

Well there is a tactile association I think eventually, because, if I did this and I did this, adjusting the position, that’s a whole step. So I mean, but there is a — but you can’t just go by that because what if one of the strings break. So you can’t all of a sudden everything fell apart. Your comfort zone, so that means you were just learning it a little bit, peripherally, it wasn’t really, you didn’t really hear. And that too is another way to kind of catapult you into learning something which you thought you knew. But I’m really adamant, I think my career has grown because I can retain something and then develop that. And I tell my students we have the unique ability to completely sabotage every band that we play in, immediately, if we lose the time or we hiccup with the time, or if the notes, all of a sudden you’re not clear with the pitch. So that’s what I mean about the clarity of the sound. The sound of a song. Not the chord changes of the song. Because Hank Jones could play the song and he would play a lot of different voicings and things, every chorus, and it would be really different, but the sound of the song was always there, © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

because he has so many choices that he has learned how to play and give the illusion that other things are happening. So I’ve had the great pleasure of being taxed and taught and embraced by all these guys that have helped me become a better player.
